summary: This document describes how to obtain IPv4 configuration dynamically in IPv6 networks by carrying DHCPv4 messages over DHCPv6 transport. It defines two new DHCPv6 messages and two new DHCPv6 options, so users on IPv6-only uplinks can still get IPv4 settings.

eli5.summary: Some people still speak only the old language, even in a new country. This RFC lets the old-style address-request message ride inside a new-style message so older setups still work.

questions: get ipv4 config on ipv6-only network
what is the dhcp 4o6 unicast flag
how does a dhcp 4o6 client find its server
subtitle: How a device on an IPv6-only uplink gets its IPv4 settings by tunnelling DHCPv4 messages inside DHCPv6.

tldr.problem: Networks are moving to IPv6, but users still need IPv4 configuration even when the uplink to their provider supports only IPv6, so ordinary DHCPv4 cannot reach the server.
tldr.mechanism: The client wraps an unchanged DHCPv4 message in a DHCPv4 Message option inside a new DHCPv6 message called DHCPv4-query, and the server answers with a DHCPv4-response built the same way.
tldr.outcome: IPv4 addresses and other DHCPv4 parameters can be handed out over an IPv6-only network while reusing existing DHCPv4 infrastructure. It is meant as a special-purpose mechanism, not something every node should enable.

today: RFC 7341 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of this DHCPv4-over-DHCPv6 transport.

sections.title: Why IPv4 Settings Over IPv6
sections.content:
As networks move to IPv6, some will be IPv6-only, yet IPv4 connectivity will keep being offered as a service over them. A client of that service needs an IPv4 address and often other IPv4 parameters, such as the addresses of IPv4-only services.

DHCPv4-over-DHCPv6 (DHCP 4o6) is a transport for exactly this. It carries DHCPv4 messages using the DHCPv6 protocol, and it reuses the existing DHCPv4 infrastructure such as failover, DNS updates and DHCP Leasequery. When IPv6 multicast carries the messages, the operator also learns about the underlying IPv6 network from the DHCPv6 relay agents the request passed through.

The RFC stresses that this is not universally applicable. It is a special-purpose mechanism for nodes that must get IPv4 configuration where native DHCPv4 is not available. Nodes that do not need it are expected not to implement it, or not to enable it by default. It can be switched on by an administrative control or automatically by a dual-stack transition mechanism, which the RFC leaves out of scope.
sections.eli5: Some networks only speak the new language, IPv6, but people still need old-style IPv4 settings. This lets the old request travel inside a new-style message.

sections.title: Architecture: Client, Relay and Server
sections.content:
The typical case is a client whose uplink supports IPv6 only, in a provider network that supports IPv6 and limited IPv4 services. The client can use only IPv6 to reach IPv4 services, so IPv4 configuration has to travel over IPv6. The RFC uses a CPE (customer premises equipment) as its example client, but any device that needs IPv4 configuration could do the same.

The DHCP 4o6 client sends a new DHCPv6 message, DHCPv4-query, carrying a DHCPv4 message. It goes either directly to the DHCP 4o6 server or through DHCPv6 relay agents. The server replies with DHCPv4-response. The relay encapsulation is used only to deliver DHCPv4 packets to a DHCPv4-capable server. It does not allocate IPv6 addresses or give the client any IPv6 configuration.

The mechanism does not limit the carried messages to DHCPv4. Because a DHCPv4 message is a special kind of BOOTP message, BOOTP messages (RFC 951) MAY be carried the same way.

Before applying for an IPv4 address, the client must pick a suitable network interface for it. How it does so is out of scope.
sections.eli5: The client hands its question to a helper (the relay) in the new envelope, and the helper passes it to the server that knows the answer. Nothing about the helper changes the question.

sections.title: New Messages and Options
sections.content:
Two new DHCPv6 messages are defined: DHCPV4-QUERY (type 20), sent by the client, and DHCPV4-RESPONSE (type 21), sent by the server. Both share one layout: an 8-bit msg-type, a 24-bit flags field, then options. The options MUST include the DHCPv4 Message option, and may include only DHCPv6 options for IPv4 configuration. They MUST NOT contain options related solely to IPv6.

In DHCPV4-QUERY only one flag bit is used, the Unicast flag U. The remaining bits are MBZ: set to zero when sending and ignored when receiving. In DHCPV4-RESPONSE the server sets every flag bit to 0 and the client ignores the field.

Two new options are defined. The DHCPv4 Message option (OPTION_DHCPV4_MSG, 87) holds a whole DHCPv4 message without any IP or UDP headers. The DHCP 4o6 Server Address option (OPTION_DHCP4_O_DHCP6_SERVER, 88) lists the IPv6 addresses of DHCP 4o6 servers, as a multiple of 16 octets. It may be empty, with a minimum length of 0.
sections.eli5: There are two new kinds of letter, one for asking and one for answering. Each has a small box on the front for notes and an inner pocket that holds the old-style form.

sections.title: Discovering Whether to Use DHCP 4o6
sections.content:
The client first MUST get its IPv6 configuration from a DHCPv6 server. It asks for the DHCP 4o6 Server Address option by listing it in an Option Request option in every Solicit, Request, Renew, Rebind and Information-request message (RFC 3315).

If the server includes the option, the client may use DHCP 4o6. If not, the client MUST NOT. If the IPv6 configuration containing the option expires, or a renewed one lacks it, the client MUST stop using DHCP 4o6 for IPv4 configuration, though it keeps asking for the option as long as it wants the service.

An empty option means the client MUST send its requests to the All_DHCP_Relay_Agents_and_Servers multicast address. A list means the client SHOULD send to each unique address. If DHCPv4 (RFC 2131) is in use on the interface where the option arrived, the client MUST stop using the IPv4 configuration obtained that way and MUST NOT use plain DHCPv4 there while the option keeps arriving. It MAY send a DHCPRELEASE first.

With several active DHCPv6 configurations (multihoming), an implementation may treat them as independent or as exclusive, keeping one active at a time. The RFC leaves the choice to the implementation.
sections.eli5: The client only uses the special envelope if its network says it may. If the permission goes away, it goes back to not using it.

sections.title: How the Client Talks to the Server
sections.content:
The client builds a DHCPv4 message and stores it verbatim in exactly one DHCPv4 Message option in a DHCPv4-query. It MUST NOT ask for the DHCP 4o6 Server Address option inside that message. When the answer arrives, the client looks for a DHCPv4 Message option, discards the response if there is none, and otherwise processes the inner message as in RFC 2131. Retransmission follows normal DHCPv4 rules, since no separate transmission parameters exist for the new message.

The Unicast flag exists because the outer IPv6 address says nothing about how the inner DHCPv4 message would have been sent. A DHCPv4 client in the RENEWING state would unicast, while one in REBINDING would broadcast. The client MUST set the flag to 1 if the message would have been unicast over IPv4 and to 0 if it would have been broadcast. It reflects how the DHCPv4 packet would have been sent, not how the DHCPv6 packet is sent.

Source addresses must have appropriate scope. For multicast the client MUST use a link-local source address. The client MUST implement RFC 4361 and send a client identifier option. For stateless IPv6 configuration it MUST refresh the server list using RFC 4242 rules.
sections.eli5: The client writes its old-style form as usual and ticks a box saying whether it would normally have shouted to everyone or spoken to one server. That helps the server understand the situation.

sections.title: Relay and Server Behavior
sections.content:
A relay that does not recognize DHCPv4-query MUST forward it as an unknown message (RFC 7283). A relay that does recognize it MAY use a separate set of destinations for these messages. A DHCPV4-QUERY goes to the configured DHCP 4o6 server addresses as a normal DHCPv6 packet, and every other type is forwarded under RFC 3315. Separate destinations are only considered for the relay closest to the client.

A server discards a query that lacks the DHCPv4 Message option, and MAY notify an administrator. Because the inner message lacks details a DHCPv4 server normally uses, such as giaddr, the server assigns addresses by local policy. If the query came via a relay, it MAY use the link-address field of the Relay-forward message to pick the IPv4 subnet. For a directly connected client it MAY use the IPv6 source address.

The server SHOULD use the flags field when forming its reply. It puts the reply in a DHCPv4 Message option inside a DHCPv4-response. A query received directly MUST be answered by unicast from the interface it arrived on. One received in a Relay-forward is answered with a Relay-reply. The server acting as a DHCPv4 relay to a normal server is left as future work.
sections.eli5: Helpers along the way either pass the new envelope on or send it to a special address. The server opens it, picks an address from the right pool, and replies the same way.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
Because DHCPv4 messages travel inside DHCPv6, an attacker could use this encapsulation to slip other messages past firewalls or network authentication gateways. The RFC judges this no more severe than current DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 practice.

A rogue server could send a Server Address option full of duplicate IPv6 addresses to cause an amplification attack. So the client MUST check for duplicates and MUST ignore all but the first instance of each address.

Enabling DHCP 4o6 also lets the DHCPv6 server shut off DHCPv4, and so IPv4, traffic on that interface. It should be enabled only where a clear trust relationship exists. A CPE can safely enable it on its WAN interface, the RFC reasons, because an ISP is unlikely to misconfigure it and an attacker is unlikely to set up a rogue DHCPv6 server in the ISP network.

IANA allocated option codes 87 and 88 and message types 20 and 21 in the DHCPv6 parameters registry.
sections.eli5: A sneaky sender might hide notes in the new envelope, or send a long list of repeated addresses. The client ignores repeats and should use this only with a network it trusts.

fields.name: flags
fields.desc: In a query, the first bit is the Unicast flag and the rest must be zero.
